tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 10(10) 2017 paper whose Sec 6.1 benchmarks Mison against RapidJSON (plus Jackson and Gson). It reports Mison 5.5-9.1x faster than the best competitor on Twitter Q1-Q8 (Fig. 8) and states the CPU (Xeon E5-1620 v3). No code, compiler or flags are published, so it cannot be A. Under this verifier's rubric that is B, the same tier the wave-3 no-code ASPLOS paper StreamTok received.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper Sec 6.1.1 / Fig. 8 (Twitter, Q1-Q8, single thread, throughput in GB/s): 'Mison is between 5.5 and 9.1 times faster than the best competitor in this experiment. The best case for Mison (8~9X) is for simple queries on mandatory fields (Q1-Q4)'. RapidJSON is one of the three competitors, so Mison is at least 5.5x faster than RapidJSON on Q1-Q8 (derived from page data; in the Fig. 8 bars Jackson, not RapidJSON, is the best competitor). Sec 6.1.2 (Fig. 9, GitHub dataset, all 31 fields, no projection push-down): Mison 'still outperforms the best existing JSON parser (Jackson) by a factor of 2'. Sec 6.1.4 / Fig. 11 (Twitter, first+last field query): basic (non-speculative) Mison beats Jackson by 3.6x, speculative Mison by 10.2x.
corrections.hardware: 3.5GHz Intel Xeon E5-1620 v3 (the paper calls it 'Broadwell-EP'), 16GB DDR3, 64-bit Windows 10; single-threaded runs with the JSON data preloaded into memory (I/O excluded)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Mison is a C++ static library; the first structural-index step uses 256-bit AVX2 SIMD and the bit-parallel steps use 64-bit instructions. The paper does not state the compiler, its version, or the flags for Mison or RapidJSON, nor the JVM version used for Jackson and Gson.
corrections.workload: Single-threaded field-projection queries over real-world JSON loaded into memory: Twitter Q1-Q8 (records have 25-30 top-level fields and a nested user object of 37-38 fields), Yelp business records (16 top-level fields), and GitHub user records (31 fixed fields). The paper compares parsing throughput (GB/s) of Mison against Gson, Jackson and RapidJSON, each using its streaming-mode API. It also runs TPC-H queries through Spark with Mison vs Jackson.
corrections.caveats: No official Mison source was found: the MSR publication page and the paper link no code or artifact. Only unofficial reimplementations exist, none benchmarked against the paper: pikkr/pikkr (Rust, 641 stars, MIT), ubnt-intrepid/misosoup (Rust, 9 stars), leocassarani/mison (Rust, 10 stars, no license), Anghagaed/MISON (21 stars, no license) and indiependente/gomison (Go, 0 stars). The compiler and flags are unstated, and in Fig. 8 RapidJSON (SAX/streaming API on Windows) is slower than Java's Jackson, so the C++ comparison point may not be well tuned. The paper calls the E5-1620 v3 'Broadwell-EP', but v3 Xeon E5 parts are Haswell-EP (a 2014-era CPU). The speedups rely on projection/filter push-down; when all fields are parsed the gain drops to about 2x over Jackson.

notes: I raised the tier from C to B. The search prompt (faster-than-std-agent-prompt.md:97) says no-code papers go in as C, but this verifier rubric makes a peer-reviewed paper B, and the wave-3 StreamTok precedent (no code) was B. If the orchestrator wants the no-code cap to win, set C. All quoted numbers (5.5-9.1x, 8-9x, 2x, 3.6x, 10.2x) appear verbatim in the paper. The only error was the figure reference for the 2x claim: it is Sec 6.1.2 / Fig. 9, not Fig. 10.

tier_reason: First-party README tables compare orjson with CPython's stdlib json, and every latency and ratio in the record matches them. The benchmark code is public (script/pybench runs bench/benchmark_dumps.py and benchmark_loads.py under pytest-benchmark), and Python 3.11.10 plus the exact PyPI wheel are stated. It is not A because no CPU model is given (only 'x86-64-v4') and the Rust toolchain that built the wheel is not stated.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Measured with the prebuilt PyPI wheel orjson-3.10.11-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux2014_x86_64.whl under CPython 3.11.10. The Rust toolchain and flags used to build that wheel are not stated. The README's recommended build is `maturin build --release --strip`, which today needs Rust >= 1.95, and the README notes that nightly Rust gives a significant performance benefit.
corrections.caveats: The baseline is Python's stdlib json module, not RapidJSON, nlohmann, simdjson or serde_json, so baseline_in_list=false. The numbers are first-party (orjson's own README) and reproducible with the published pybench script, but the CPU is given only as x86-64-v4, with no model. The benchmark used orjson 3.10.11, while the current release is 3.12.0 (2026-08-14). The license is mixed OSI: much of src/ is MPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft) and the rest is Apache-2.0 OR MIT; GitHub reports only Apache-2.0. orjson ships only as a Python module, not a Rust crate.

notes: All eight median-latency rows and ratios in claimed_speedup match the README verbatim. The latest commit on the default branch (master) is 2026-08-14. The record's 2026-09-14 is the repo pushed_at date, not a master commit. Stars are 8,234; not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: First-party benchmarks README states in text only that reflect-cpp is 'usually about twice as fast' as RapidJSON and 'about 10 times faster' than nlohmann/json, with no measured values. The public benchmark code (benchmarks/json/{canada,licenses,person}.cpp, Google Benchmark vs nlohmann, RapidJSON, simdjson and yyjson) runs only in CI, whose results sit in job step summaries, and no CPU model is given, so the tier is C.

corrections.workload: Read-only benchmark (parse JSON into typed C++ structs) on three datasets: canada (float-heavy), licenses (nested, string-heavy) and person (small). It compares reflect-cpp (yyjson backend, one-line rfl::json::read) against hand-written nlohmann/json, RapidJSON, simdjson (skipped on clang) and yyjson code with Google Benchmark (benchmarks/json/*.cpp). Writes are benchmarked only in the separate cross-format suite (benchmarks/all).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt sets -std=c++20 -Wall -O2 (MSVC: -std:c++20 -O2) and the README builds with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release. The README's 'gcc 11.4 on Ubuntu 22.4' note applies only to the depicted cross-format charts. The JSON-library comparison runs in CI (.github/workflows/linux.yaml 'benchmarks' jobs, gcc 11-14 and clang 16-18), with results written only to GitHub Actions job step summaries.
corrections.hardware: Not stated on the page; the CI benchmark jobs run on GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runners (CPU model not stated)
corrections.caveats: The page has no measured numbers for the RapidJSON and nlohmann comparison, only the text summary ('usually about twice as fast', 'about 10 times faster'). The PNG charts in benchmarks/img compare reflect-cpp's own formats (flexbuf, msgpack, bson, json, cbor, toml, yaml, xml) against each other, not against other JSON libraries. Per-run numbers exist only in GitHub Actions job step summaries, which are not in the job logs. No CPU model is given. The comparison is first-party, and reflect-cpp's JSON speed comes from its embedded yyjson backend; the README says it is slightly slower than simdjson and yyjson.

notes: The claimed_speedup quotes are accurate. The record's caveat was wrong that the PNG charts show the RapidJSON and nlohmann results: they are cross-format charts. Metadata checks out: MIT, 1,937 stars, last commit 2026-09-22, not archived, not a fork. rfl.getml.com/benchmarks repeats the same text claims, also without numbers.
